item.title: Sen Ron Johnson talks Fauci emails, new Senate filibuster strategy on 'Ruthless'
item.description: Sen. Ron Johnson said he wants to hold Anthony Fauci accountable for a "failed" COVID response during an interview with the "Ruthless" podcast released Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., gave the latest update on what he described as an effort to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci "accountable" for his controversial handling of the COVID-19 pandemic and detailed his new filibuster strategy for the Senate in a new interview with the "Ruthless" podcast.

"I think our response to COVID was a miserably failed response, freedom robbing," Johnson said in an exclusive interview released Tuesday morning. "It didn't work. I mean, it simply didn't work. And the fact that Fauci has skated now for six years without accountability, this begins that accountability." 

In his role as chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Johnson authored a report alleging the Biden administration misled the American public during the pandemic. 

IOWA GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL ZACH LAHN TELLS 'RUTHLESS' DEMOCRATS ARE HIDING THEIR BAD POLICIES

The interview took place just days after the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, led by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., released Fauci’s daily journal entries. In the journal, Fauci chronicles his rapid rise to celebrity status, interactions with the Trump and Biden teams as they grappled with the pandemic, and his thoughts on the virus' origins, which remains a point of dispute. 

Fauci will testify in a Senate Homeland Security hearing on Wednesday. Fauci's handling of the pandemic, his guidance on public health measures and lockdowns, his views on what started the virus, and the U.S.' alleged ties to the Chinese lab thought by some to be the cause of the crisis, have been major points of contention for Republicans. 

As director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), Fauci served on the COVID task forces under Presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden, and he was the latter's chief medical advisor until stepping down in 2022.

"I appreciate Chairman Paul calling this hearing, doggedly getting the documents," Johnson told the podcast. "Again, it's like pulling teeth getting these documents. Yeah, we finally got some hard drives, whatever those little thumb drives are called, with some of the information from some of his devices… I think there's still a lot more documents to uncover."

‘FINISH THE DAMN JOB’: HAGERTY TELLS 'RUTHLESS PODCAST' THAT TRUMP WILL COMPLETE IRAN MISSION

Johnson, who recently took the gavel atop the Senate Budget Committee following the death of South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, also outlined a new strategy for putting Democrats on record over the upper chamber’s filibuster process.

In the interview, he said that if Democrats gain back full control of Congress, they could eliminate the filibuster mechanism and pass a slate of left-wing priorities on a simple party-line basis. He then suggested a plan to put the opposition on record.

"The only way I can see Democrats not ending the filibuster is if you have to get them on the record voting not to end it," Johnson said. "Make sure that it is hard-and-fast Senate rule that you can only end the filibuster with 67 votes. You can't do it using the nuclear option."

item.title: DNA cracks centuries-old murder mystery involving one of history's most famous families
item.description: Ancient DNA from the Medici brothers' remains revealed a novel malaria strain, offering scientific proof against longstanding poisoning rumors, researchers say.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers at Yale University believe they've solved a centuries-old mystery over how a member of one of Italy's most famous families died.

In a study published in the journal iScience, researchers analyzed ancient DNA from Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici, the Renaissance ruler of Tuscany, who died suddenly in 1587.

Francesco I de' Medici and his wife, Bianca Cappello, died a day apart after falling ill with intermittent fevers following a stay at a mosquito-filled villa — fueling centuries of rumors that they had been poisoned.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Working with paleopathologists from the University of Pisa in Italy, the team analyzed DNA extracted from the ribs of Francesco I de' Medici, as well as Giovanni de' Medici, his younger brother who died of malaria 25 years earlier.

The research was led by Serena Tucci, assistant professor of anthropology at Yale University, whose work was publicized in a university press release on June 30.

Researchers found genetic traces of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite responsible for the deadliest form of malaria — effectively debunking the longstanding poisoning theory.

The team "found a novel strain of Plasmodium falciparum, the species that causes the deadliest form of human malaria, in the bones of Giovanni de Medici," the release said.

ANCIENT ROMAN VILLA BENEATH HIGH SCHOOL GYM REVEALS STUNNING SECRET FROM THE PAST

"The researchers also discovered molecular traces of P. falciparum and a second species, P. malariae, in the remains of Francesco de Medici," the statement added.

While malaria was endemic to central Italy during the Renaissance, the lack of definitive scientific evidence allowed theories to persist.

"Their quick deaths spawned rumors that Francesco’s brother and rival, Cardinal Ferdinando de Medici, had them poisoned with arsenic," said the statement.

It marks the first time researchers have genetically analyzed the brothers' skeletal remains, confirming earlier evidence they had malaria.

SHAKESPEARE'S MISSING LONDON HOME PINPOINTED AFTER CENTURIES-LONG MYSTERY, RESEARCHER SAYS

The results are "scientific proof to dispel persistent speculation that Francesco de Medici was poisoned to death," Yale officials said.

Archival sources, including contemporary reports from court physicians, describe the symptoms the brothers suffered that are consistent with malaria, which was called "febbre terzana" by residents of Central Italy at the time.

"The reports also describe the treatments to which the stricken were subjected, including bloodletting, a common practice that likely did patients more harm than good," the release said.

Although historical records described symptoms consistent with malaria, rumors that Francesco had been poisoned persisted for centuries, Tucci told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Asked why the rumors persisted, Tucci said, "We do not know."

The professor added, "Probably because it was still plausible, given that up to now, there were no conclusive reports that indeed they had malaria. Our study is the first one to genetically confirm it."

Tucci added that while the researchers cannot completely rule out poisoning, "malaria remains the most likely explanation for his cause of death."

She also noted that "the hypothesis of poisoning doesn't seem to be well-supported from a scientific perspective — it's very speculative."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"We can only say that we found the pathogen that causes malaria in this specimen, confirming that he had malaria," Tucci said.

The same genetic approach could "certainly" help solve other historical mysteries, said Gisella Caccone, a senior research scientist in Yale's Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology and a co-author of the study.

"[It's possible if] there is a clear hypothesis to address and one can address it using genomic-based approaches," added Caccone. "It depends on the questions and the tools we have."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The DNA recovered from centuries-old remains can do more than solve historical mysteries, Caccone pointed out: The newly identified malaria strain could help researchers better understand how the parasite has evolved over time.

"The more we know about how fast it can change, the better our methods and models to control will be," she noted.

"Using historical specimens can not only help us understand our past better, but also it can help build a better future."

item.title: NFL legend Drew Brees reveals the shocking reason he passed on Nick Saban and the Dolphins
item.description: Drew Brees revealed on the "New Heights" podcast how Miami's 25% medical projection and a post-Katrina drive through New Orleans changed his career.
item.content:encoded:
NFL legend Drew Brees appeared on the "New Heights" podcast and broke down the crazy story of his 2006 free agency. It turns out a failed medical evaluation and an upside-down Chevy truck in a living room changed football history forever.

Back in 2006, coming off a severe shoulder injury in San Diego, the Miami Dolphins looked like a done deal.

"On paper, it was Miami all the way. Miami had Nick Saban. They had just come off a 9-7 season. Defense was lights out. They were running the same offense we were running."

NICK SABAN URGES SENATE TO PASS LEGISLATION TO FIX COLLEGE SPORTS, BUT COACHING CONTRACTS GLOSSED OVER

Former Dolphins owner Wayne Huizenga rolled out the red carpet to lure Brees to Miami.

"I’m sitting there eating dinner on Wayne Huizenga’s yacht. He’s talking about playing golf in Scotland every summer. No state income tax. I’m like, 'Dude, this is wallpaper. Miami, here I come.'"

Then the Dolphins' medical staff changed everything.

DOLPHINS CHEERLEADERS MAKE MAJOR MOVES TO COMPETE WITH COWBOYS CHEERLEADERS, TEBOWS GET OUT & RYAN CLARK!

"I’m in Miami in an MRI tube for two hours just aching. They stick these big needles in my shoulder to test the nerve endings. I got this feeling of doubt. They don't really think I will be able to play. Their doctors said I had a 25% chance of coming back and playing again."

Miami saw too much risk. New Orleans saw a franchise quarterback.

"New Orleans was six months post-Katrina. They just hired some unknown head coach named Sean Payton. Who is this guy?"

NICK SABAN URGES SENATE TO PASS LEGISLATION TO FIX COLLEGE SPORTS, BUT COACHING CONTRACTS GLOSSED OVER

While Miami doubted him, the Saints went all in.

"I go to New Orleans and it was like, 'You are our guy.' Sean Payton and Mickey Loomis said, 'We’re building this offense around you.'"

"They did everything they could to roll out the red carpet despite all the circumstances. New Orleans was still destroyed."

The city was still reeling six months after Hurricane Katrina. Brees took a drive through town and couldn't believe what he saw.

"Houses were off their foundations. There was a Chevy truck upside down in a living room. The car stops, and there’s a tugboat in the middle of the road."

"I’m looking at my wife like, 'Are you seeing what I’m seeing?'"

That was the moment everything flipped. "It was one of those moments where it's like this is so much bigger than just football. We get to be part of the resurrection of one of America’s greatest cities."

"This is God’s calling in our life. And that was the determining factor."

As NFL history would show, Brees made the right call. He won a Super Bowl in New Orleans.

Miami traded for Daunte Culpepper instead, and Nick Saban fled to Alabama to build a college dynasty.

All because of a failed medical evaluation and a leap of faith.

item.title: Kash Patel's attorney rejects The Atlantic's effort to dismiss defamation lawsuit, vows 'accountability'
item.description: The attorney for FBI Director Kash Patel slammed The Atlantic's filing aiming to dismiss his $250 million defamation lawsuit against the magazine.
item.content:encoded:
The attorney for FBI Director Kash Patel fired back at The Atlantic on Monday over its effort to dismiss his defamation lawsuit against the magazine.

Patel filed a $250 million suit in April accusing The Atlantic and its staff writer Sarah Fitzpatrick of publishing a "defamatory hit piece," outlining claims of drunken behavior as the FBI chief, which he has denied.

The Atlantic both filed a motion to dismiss the suit and a motion to stay discovery on Monday "except Touhy requests" in the U.S. District Court for Washington, D.C. Touhy requests seek "any official information for litigation purposes, including witnesses and documents, when the Government is not a party to the litigation," according to a definition shared by Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General.

"It’s truly incredible that The Atlantic wants one-sided discovery so that it can shield its own so-called 'sources' while being able to rummage through government documents unimpeded," Patel's attorney Jesse Binnall told Fox News Digital. "This again shows that they are afraid of the truth and believe they are above the law."

"We intend to prove them wrong and bring accountability to the fake news," Binnall added.

FBI DIRECTOR KASH PATEL VOWS TO TAKE THE ATLANTIC TO COURT OVER 'DEFAMATORY' REPORT

The filing said Patel "brings this defamation action against The Atlantic for publishing an undeniably newsworthy article about his job performance that he finds politically inconvenient." It also calls out the FBI director's other defamation lawsuits against other outlets, claiming he "sends an ominous message to the press: publishing reporting that he does not like comes at a high cost," adding, "These tactics strike at the very foundation of the First Amendment."

"The Motion to Dismiss filed today by The Atlantic explains why this lawsuit is meritless and should be dismissed as a matter of law," The Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg said in a statement. "We are simultaneously asking the court to permit us to begin seeking factual discovery from the FBI and the Department of Justice – including documents and depositions of key individuals – that is appropriate given the allegations in this matter."

Goldberg continued, "If Director Patel did not want to face this process, he should not have filed this suit. These legal filings are consistent with the promise I made to our staff and to our readers in May: we will defend The Atlantic and its staff vigorously; we will not be intimidated by acts of politically motivated retaliation; we will continue to cover the FBI professionally, fairly, and thoroughly; and we will continue to practice journalism in the public interest."

THE ATLANTIC REPORTER BEHIND KASH PATEL REPORT SAYS SHE'S SINCE BEEN 'INUNDATED' BY SOURCES REAFFIRMING CLAIMS

The FBI's rapid response team on X issued a statement slamming The Atlantic for "propagating false narratives because it has zero interest in any form of real journalism" and that it "adds no value to society except as the leading slop rag of the day."

The Atlantic's story, "The FBI Director is MIA," outlined several serious allegations, including instances of erratic behavior, "excessive drinking" and "unexplained absences."

The first claim alleged Patel had a "freak-out" over a tech issue in April when attempting to log into a computer system, believing he was being fired by President Donald Trump after Attorney General Pam Bondi's ouster and had to prepare an announcement. The Atlantic cited nine unnamed sources familiar with the alleged incident.

"But Patel, according to multiple current officials, as well as former officials who have stayed close to him, is deeply concerned that his job is in jeopardy. He has good reasons to think so — including some having to do with what witnesses described to me as bouts of excessive drinking," Fitzpatrick told readers before citing past reports of rumors that Patel was also on the chopping block.

"The IT-lockout episode is emblematic of Patel’s tumultuous tenure as director of the FBI: He is erratic, suspicious of others, and prone to jumping to conclusions before he has necessary evidence, according to the more than two dozen people I interviewed about Patel’s conduct, including current and former FBI officials, staff at law-enforcement and intelligence agencies, hospitality-industry workers, members of Congress, political operatives, lobbyists, and former advisers," Fitzpatrick wrote.

HOUSE DEMOCRATS DEMAND KASH PATEL TAKE ALCOHOL TEST UNDER PENALTY OF PERJURY AFTER ATLANTIC REPORT

The report alleged that Patel has a pattern of "conspicuous inebriation" and that "he is known to drink to the point of obvious intoxication" in spots in Washington, D.C., and Las Vegas. The report also alleged that early in his tenure, some meetings and briefings had to be pushed to later in the day as a "result of his alcohol-fueled nights."

"On multiple occasions in the past year, members of his security detail had difficulty waking Patel because he was seemingly intoxicated, according to information supplied to Justice Department and White House officials," the report alleged.

Unnamed sources also speculated whether Patel's alcohol consumption played a role in his social media posts that shared inaccurate information about active law enforcement investigations, including what he had written after Charlie Kirk's assassination before suspect Tyler Robinson turned himself in last September. 

The FBI forcefully pushed back against the report, and multiple members of the Trump administration, including White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, expressed their support for Patel.

"Print it, all false, I’ll see you in court — bring your checkbook," Patel told The Atlantic in a statement included in the report.

item.title: What your internet provider, websites and advertisers see
item.description: Your internet provider, websites and advertisers can track your browsing activity even without you posting online. Here's how to limit what they see.
item.content:encoded:
Most people assume that if they are not posting on social media or sharing personal information online, they are staying relatively private. Unfortunately, that isn't how today's internet works.

Every time you browse the web, multiple companies can collect information about you. Your internet provider can monitor certain parts of your online activity, websites can gather data about your visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles based on your browsing habits.

The good news? Knowing what others can see is the first step toward protecting your privacy.

AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Your internet service provider, or ISP, acts as the middleman between your devices and the internet. Every website you visit and every online service you use passes through its network.

If you are not using a VPN, your ISP can generally see which websites you are connecting to, when you are online, how much data you are using and your approximate location based on your IP address. Encrypted websites, which begin with "https://," help prevent your provider from reading the contents of most web pages or messages. However, your ISP can still often see that you connected to a certain website in the first place. That information alone can reveal a lot about your interests, routines and habits.

Even if you never create an account, some websites can still learn quite a bit about your visit. They can identify your IP address, estimate your location, determine what device and browser you are using and record which pages you viewed.

Some websites also use analytics tools, tracking pixels and advertising scripts to understand how visitors interact with their pages. These tools can show what links you clicked, how long you stayed and which content got your attention.

In some cases, this information may also be shared with advertising or analytics companies. That is one reason you may see ads that seem closely connected to something you recently searched for, viewed or clicked.

ARE APPLE DEVICES SPYING? WHAT YOUR IPHONE TRACKS

Private browsing tabs, also known as incognito mode in some browsers, can be useful. They help prevent your browser from saving your local browsing history after you close the window.

However, private browsing does not make you invisible online. Websites can still see your visit while you are on their pages. Your internet provider can still see many of the sites you connect to. If you are using a work, school or public network, the network owner may also be able to monitor certain activity.

Private browsing is better thought of as a local privacy tool. It helps hide activity from someone else using the same device later, but it does not fully hide you from websites, advertisers or your internet provider while you are online.

How to reduce what others can see

You cannot eliminate online tracking entirely, but you can make it harder for companies to collect information about you. Start by reviewing your browser's privacy settings. Turn off unnecessary website permissions, such as location, microphone and camera access for sites that do not need them. Consider using a privacy-focused browser or search engine that collects less personal data.

You can also check out these 11 easy ways to protect your online privacy for more ways to limit online tracking. You should also limit how much personal information you share online. The more details you provide across websites, apps and accounts, the easier it becomes for companies to connect your activity. Most importantly, consider using a VPN.

A VPN, or virtual private network, encrypts your internet traffic before it leaves your device. Instead of your internet provider seeing which websites you are connecting to, it sees an encrypted connection to the VPN server. That makes it much harder for your ISP to build a browsing profile based on your online activity.

A VPN can also help protect your information on public Wi-Fi networks and mask your IP address from websites, advertisers and other third parties. However, a VPN does not stop every type of online tracking. Websites may still recognize you when you log in to an account, use the same browser or share personal details.

A solid VPN makes this process easier by offering apps for computers, smartphones, tablets, smart TVs and routers. That allows you to protect multiple devices with one account.

The internet is built around data, and several companies can collect information every time you browse. Internet providers can see where you are connecting, websites can monitor visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles over time. You cannot disappear completely, but you can reduce what others learn about you. A few privacy-minded habits, combined with a trusted VPN, can help you take back more control of your online activity.

item.title: Monica Lewinsky's Lindsey Graham tribute draws criticism and praise for placing people over party: expert
item.description: Experts say Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham after his death reflects her philosophy of people over party despite political disagreements.
item.content:encoded:
Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham following his death sparked interest across the aisles, not only for her respectful candor, but also served as a reminder of the late senator's impact on history.

Lewinsky, 53, paid her respects to the late South Carolina senator shortly after his death earlier this month and gave followers insight on their decades-long connection.

Her non-partisan testimonial drew criticism online, but experts believed that her tribute was an authentic gesture which reflected her personal philosophy of people over party.

MONICA LEWINSKY RECALLS 'VERY DARK MOMENTS' AFTER SCANDAL, SURVIVING JUDGMENT BY 'BILLIONS OF STRANGERS'

Graham, who died July 11 after what his office described was a "brief and sudden illness," was one of the Republican Party's most influential voices with more than three decades of service.

His death prompted thousands of tributes, including one poignant message from the former White House intern.

MONICA LEWINSKY SAYS BILL CLINTON ‘ESCAPED A LOT MORE THAN I DID’ AFTER WHITE HOUSE SCANDAL

"I've disagreed with many (many) of Lindsey Graham’s choices and beliefs, but he was also — as one of the house managers on the '98 impeachment — the one who worked tirelessly to prove there was a smear campaign against me from inside the WH," Lewinsky posted on X shortly after his death.

When X users took umbrage with the homage, Lewinsky was quick to remind followers that her experience was "healing" after years of trauma from the Clinton scandal.

"Come on. He did not do it for you. The man was evil," one user wrote.

Lewinsky fired back, "I know he didn’t do it for me. i didn’t whitewash his history. but those actions were healing for me (and my family)… thanks for sharing your opinion."

SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS

Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Lewinsky's tribute "fits her clearly identified personal philosophy to a tee."

"She's not suddenly a Lindsey Graham fan — she's just honest enough to say he did one thing that mattered to her, and she's not going to let political disagreement erase that," Uthe said. "It works in her favor, and it's the kind of nuance that actually means something."

Uthe noted that Lewinsky's post was "nonchalant, direct, and completely unpolished in the best way."

"There's no performance to it — it reads like: 'Hey, he wasn't perfect, I disagreed with most of what he did, but he did this one thing for me and I appreciated it.' That's it. It's classy, and it's a stand-up thing to highlight in someone's death."

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

Graham was one of the 13 House members appointed to Clinton's impeachment trial, where he not only blasted the former president for lying under oath, but also argued to restore "honor and integrity to the office."

item.title: Is drinking every day alcoholism? Experts explain where culture and addiction collide
item.description: Ed Sheeran's viral podcast clip reignites debate over British drinking culture versus American alcoholism definitions and when drinking becomes a problem.
item.content:encoded:
A clip from Ed Sheeran's appearance on "The Louis Theroux Podcast" has recently resurfaced on social media, sparking renewed debate over differences between British and American attitudes toward alcohol.

"Americans call something ‘alcoholism’ that Brits simply call ‘culture.’ Maybe one or two pints at the end of a workday," the singer said during the 2025 podcast.

"On a Friday you’ll have 6 pints and a bottle of wine. It’s not alcoholism to drink every day here … It’s just the culture."

NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS

Americans and Britons consume similar amounts of alcohol overall, with the average adult drinking about 9.7 liters of pure alcohol per year, according to the World Health Organization.

Drinking patterns — such as how often people drink, how much they consume in a single sitting and social attitudes toward alcohol — can differ even when overall consumption is similar, according to public health experts.

In the U.K., pubs are commonly regarded as community gathering places, with alcohol representing a routine part of social life for many people. In the U.S., attitudes toward drinking tend to vary more widely by region, religion and social norms, experts say.

Jessica Steinman, chief clinical officer at No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, noted that British and American cultures have always been very different, and that includes alcohol consumption.

DRINKING ALCOHOL MAY INFLUENCE CRAVINGS FOR CERTAIN FOODS IN A SURPRISING WAY, STUDY SUGGESTS

"Americans can’t legally drink until 21, and it is frowned upon to do so before that age," she told Fox News Digital. "In England, there is less stigma and restrictions around alcohol, which changes how people view it and drink it."

"Regardless of where anyone lives and regardless of their culture, when alcohol or substances start negatively affecting someone’s life or when someone cannot control the levels of alcohol they drink, then it is a problem," Steinman said.

"When drinking gets in the way of a job, school or relationships — or when people start numbing out from difficult feelings or escaping their problems through alcohol — it isn’t just cultural drinking, it’s an addiction."

Steinman said she's concerned that people with alcohol use disorder may dismiss or justify their drinking as a normal part of their local culture, making them less likely to recognize it as a problem and seek help.

Chris Tuell, EdD., clinical director of addiction services at Lindner Center of HOPE and associate professor at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, reiterated that Sheeran’s comments highlight how culture influences people’s perceptions of alcohol.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"What is considered ‘normal’ in one country may seem excessive in another," he told Fox News Digital. "In parts of the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Australia or even parts of the U.S., drinking is woven into sporting events, celebrations, work gatherings and family traditions."

Tuell noted, however, that culture does not determine whether someone has alcohol use disorder (AUD).

"The fact that something is common does not automatically make it healthy — the same principle applies to alcohol," he told Fox News Digital. "A person may live in a culture where drinking every evening is expected. Another person may rarely drink because their culture discourages alcohol altogether. Neither person's cultural background alone tells us whether alcohol is helping or hurting them."

Two people can drink exactly the same amount each week while having completely different outcomes, according to Tuell.

"One person may drink socially, maintain healthy relationships, perform well at work and easily choose not to drink when needed," he said. "Another person drinking the exact same amount may experience worsening anxiety, strained relationships, poor sleep, financial problems, declining health and an inability to stop."

Whether someone drinks every day, only on weekends or only at celebrations is only part of the picture, the expert noted.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Tuell recommends paying close attention to the following important patterns that can potentially indicate alcohol use disorder.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Ultimately, AUD is measured less by how much a person drinks and more by how much alcohol has begun to take from their life," Tuell said.

"That perspective moves us beyond stereotypes and cultural expectations. It replaces judgment with curiosity, stigma with understanding, and shame with the opportunity for honest self-reflection and meaningful change."

One of the greatest barriers to recognizing a drinking problem is comparison, according to the expert — as people might say things like "everyone I know drinks this much" or "my family drinks every day."

"Those comparisons can be misleading," Tuell said. "Imagine someone saying, ‘everyone in my family has high blood pressure.’ That doesn't make untreated hypertension healthy. Likewise, widespread drinking doesn't eliminate the possibility that alcohol is causing harm."

Anyone experiencing symptoms of alcohol use disorder should consult a healthcare provider for evaluation and guidance.

item.title: First on Fox: Trump DOJ reaches settlement with pro-life protester targeted by Biden admin
item.description: Paul Vaughn reached a seven-figure settlement with the DOJ after the FBI raided his home at gunpoint over a peaceful pro-life protest in Tennessee.
item.content:encoded:

The resolution follows a similar settlement reached by another pro-life activist, Mark Houck.

Houck received a seven-figure settlement from the Trump DOJ after filing a lawsuit over his 2022 arrest. He sought restitution for what he called "a faulty investigation" and "excessive force" after a SWAT team of around 25 people arrested him in front of his children at his home on Sept. 23, 2022, allegedly with guns drawn, on charges he had violated the FACE Act.

The shocking details of his arrest spurred criticism from conservatives that the Justice Department was targeting pro-life activists.

"Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed said, according to audio obtained by Politico. SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS

El-Sayed did not apologize for or retract the metaphor. He instead argued that senators should be willing to challenge colleagues who fail to act according to the values on which they campaigned. The progressive candidate then pivoted to accuse the United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC, of running repeated attacks against his character on Stevens’ behalf. He invoked his wife, mother and two daughters while rejecting accusations that his rhetoric toward women had been disrespectful.

"I was raised by strong women," El-Sayed said, arguing that claims he was sexist because he had criticized former first lady Michelle Obama in a years-old opinion piece and challenged Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the 2018 gubernatorial primary were "inconsistent with the truth."

Stevens responded by highlighting other comments attributed to El-Sayed during the leaked donor call, including attacks involving Whitmer, former Sen. Debbie Stabenow and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was in the race with El-Sayed and Stevens before dropping out earlier this month.

"Only he can account for saying that Whitmer is bought and paid for, or that no one cares about Debbie Stabenow, or that Mallory McMorrow isn’t smart enough," Stevens said.

She later delivered a pointed response to El-Sayed’s clarification.

"Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre," Stevens said.

MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT MALLORY MCMORROW DROPS OUT OF SENATE RACE WEEKS BEFORE PRIMARY

Meanwhile, Stevens' campaign spokesperson, Arik Wolk, accused El-Sayed of resorting to personal insults and focusing on his national political ambitions rather than Michigan.

"Abdul continues with personal insults and making this race about his personal political ambitions and the other 49 states," Wolk said. "Haley is focused on getting things done for Michigan, and only Michigan."

Republicans also took advantage of the remarks. RNC Research characterized El-Sayed’s debate response as a "double down" on calling Fetterman an "ogre," while Michigan Republican strategist Dennis Lennox argued that El-Sayed’s candidacy was "about propelling the hard Left’s ascent nationally."

The "pike" imagery has triggered political controversy before. In 2020, former Trump White House strategist Steve Bannon said he would place the heads of Dr. Anthony Fauci and then-FBI Director Christopher Wray "on pikes" outside the White House as a warning to federal officials.

X, then-Twitter, suspended Bannon’s podcast account following backlash over the remarks, while Facebook and YouTube removed the video they were included in, citing policies addressing violent or incendiary content. Bannon later maintained that he had been speaking metaphorically — similar to El-Sayed.

Earlier that year, a separate "head on a pike" controversy erupted during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial after CBS News reported that an unnamed Trump confidant said Republican senators had been warned, "Vote against the president and your head will be on a pike."

Then-House impeachment manager, now Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., repeated the report on the Senate floor while stressing, "I don’t know if that is true" and "I hope it is not true." Republican senators immediately disputed the account, with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, saying she knew of no senator who had been threatened by the administration and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, said of Schiff’s remark about the alleged comments: "That’s when he lost me."

"Not only have I never heard the ‘head on the pike’ line, but also I know of no Republican senator who has been threatened in any way by anyone in the administration," Collins told reporters at the time.

item.title: Prominent Holocaust museum challenges Mamdani with offer in response to claims about 'genocide' in Gaza
item.description: Holocaust Museum Chairman Jeff Miller invited Zohran Mamdani to visit and learn what genocide actually means after the NYC mayor's repeated use of the term.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is yet to publicly respond to an invitation from a prominent Holocaust museum to visit in order to "truly understand" what "genocide looks like" as he faces criticism from the Jewish community for repeatedly using that label to describe the situation in Gaza.

"You keep using the word ‘genocide’ when talking about Israel," Jeff Miller, chair of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, posted on X on Friday, inviting Mamdani to visit the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C.

"If you truly want to understand what genocide looks like, as Chairman of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, I would be happy to personally arrange a tour of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum for you."

Miller was responding to a post from the UJA-Federation of New York expressing grief over a pair of recent stabbings in New York City carried out by an attacker who allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" during the attacks. Authorities say one of the victims is Jewish, and the attack is being investigated as a hate crime. 

JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES

Miller’s post went on to say that "words matter especially from elected leaders" and that "rhetoric that demonizes Israel and the Jewish state has consequences."

"I hope you are simply ignoring the impact of your words and not purposely trying to normalize antisemitism," Miller wrote. "My invitation is sincere. Come to the Museum. Learn what genocide actually means."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office multiple times inquiring whether the mayor intends to take Miller up on his offer but did not receive a response.

SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK

Miller told Fox News Digital that he felt an "obligation" to speak up and that he would be "happy" to personally walk Mamdani through the museum.

"If the mayor wants to repeatedly invoke that word, I invite him to come with me to the Holocaust Museum and confront what genocide actually looked like: the systematic attempt to annihilate an entire people," Miller said. "If he does not want to come to our museum, he should visit Rwanda or another place whose people have endured genocide and listen to survivors."

Miller added that Mamdani is free to "criticize the Israeli government" and disagree with policies, "but there is a profound difference between legitimate criticism of a government and rhetoric that demonizes the world’s only Jewish state and helps normalize hostility toward Jews."

Miller’s invitation was celebrated by many on social media, including Republican Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who posted on X that he hopes Mamdani takes the offer.

MAMDANI'S LATEST NETANYAHU REMARKS DEEPEN CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH LEADERS

"The US Holocaust Memorial Museum — where I proudly serve on the Council — is an important institution that shows the truth about what happened," Scott wrote. "I urge anyone visiting Washington, DC to stop by. "

"The @NYCMayor Mamdani should take up the Chairman’s offer for a tour of the Holocaust Museum so he understands what is genocide," billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X.

Mamdani has faced intense criticism for his position on Israel since jumping into the mayoral race last year and since taking office, he has often angered the Jewish community with comments calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and repeatedly accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza after the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people," Mamdani said last week in a video announcement that he did not have the authority to arrest Netanyahu in accordance with an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant, a warrant the United States does not recognize.

"He is responsible for the killing of more than 73,000 people, for the maiming of tens of thousands of children as those who survive undergo amputation without anesthesia. For the targeting of neonatal hospitals and maternity care centers, denying newborns even the chance to live. For the countless people he starved as he blocked food and humanitarian aid from reaching them. For the gunning down of hundreds of aid workers and journalists."

item.title: Freed American reveals brutal Iran prison ordeal, warns hostages face greater danger
item.description: Morad Tahbaz describes harsh Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps detention in Evin Prison and warns that the U.S.-Iran war could make Americans still held in Tehran more vulnerable.
item.content:encoded:
For nearly six years, American conservationist Morad Tahbaz lived in what he described as hell inside Iran’s prison system. The worst four months were spent completely alone in a small cell, beneath a bright light that never went dark.

Tahbaz was held in Ward 2A of Iran’s Evin Prison, which he described as a high-security detention facility controlled by the intelligence branch of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

He was allowed out only twice a day for about 10 minutes and was forced to wear a blindfold whenever he left, Tahbaz told Fox News Digital. His weekly call with his wife lasted only a few minutes and was monitored so closely that an official interrupted whenever he spoke in English.

"This is probably the harshest and toughest imprisonment that any prisoner will go through," Tahbaz, who was finally released in September 2023, told Fox News Digital of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence detention facility inside Iran's Evin Prison.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

Tahbaz was living and working in Iran as a conservationist when authorities arrested him alongside several colleagues in January 2018. He had co-founded the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, which worked to protect endangered species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian leopard.

One of the accusations leveled against him, Tahbaz said, was that he had trained lizards to spy on Iranian military installations for Israel.

"You can’t make this stuff up," Tahbaz said in the Zoom interview with Fox News Digital. "It just gives you an idea of the kind of narrative that this regime comes up with. They’ll come up with anything."

What began with interrogations in January 2018 turned into nearly six years of imprisonment for the Iranian American conservationist.

Now free and back in his home in the U.S., Tahbaz fears the war between the United States and Iran could make the Americans still held by Iran both more vulnerable and more valuable as negotiating assets.

"I do think the strikes in Iran will have an impact on the hostages’ situation and their circumstances," he said.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Tahbaz said he spent his first two years inside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence facility at Evin.

After his conviction, Tahbaz was transferred into the general prison population. He said his cellmates ranged from suspected ISIS members to former Iranian government ministers.

The isolation and physical conditions were accompanied by constant uncertainty.

"The uncertainty when you are a hostage is not like you think at the end of your sentence they’ll necessarily let you go," Tahbaz said. "They’ll just come up with another charge to keep you there for as long as you’re of value to them."

Tahbaz was released Sept. 18, 2023, with four other Americans in a Qatar-mediated agreement between Washington and Iran. The exchange also involved five Iranians held by the United States and the transfer of $6 billion in previously frozen Iranian funds into a restricted account for humanitarian transactions.

The negotiation brought Tahbaz home, but he believes Western governments have failed to establish consequences strong enough to stop Iran from detaining more foreign and dual nationals.

"This business of hostage-taking has been going on essentially since the beginning of the revolution," he said.

LAWYER FOR AMERICAN DETAINED IN IRAN SAYS HOSTAGE DEAL IS 'EASIEST PROBLEM ON THE TABLE' FOR BOTH SIDES

"It will continue, in my opinion, as long as there is no deterrence," Tahbaz added. "None of the Western governments, in reality, have done anything significant about stopping this practice."

The issue returned to the forefront in July with the release of Dena Karari, a 53-year-old Iranian American from California.

Karari had been unable to leave Iran since December 2024 after authorities confiscated her passports. Her attorney said she faced allegations of espionage and collaboration with a hostile state. President Donald Trump announced in July that she had been allowed to leave and called the decision a "gesture of goodwill."

Karari was not continuously imprisoned, according to reporting about her case, but she remained under an exit ban and was repeatedly interrogated.

Her release offered relief during a widening conflict, but Tahbaz said dual nationals remain particularly vulnerable because Iran does not recognize their foreign citizenship.

"Iran doesn’t recognize any other nationality other than the Iranian," he said.

Authorities can develop a national-security case, secure a sentence and then preserve the prisoner for use in future negotiations, Tahbaz said.

"You’re condemned, and they pass sentence, and you’re in the system, and now you are a bargaining chip," he said.

The precise number of Americans currently imprisoned or prevented from leaving Iran remains unclear.

Reuters reported in March that at least six U.S. citizens or permanent residents were detained in Iran, including journalist Reza Valizadeh, businessman Kamran Hekmati and U.S. permanent resident Shahab Dalili.

Valizadeh, a former Radio Farda journalist, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly collaborating with a hostile government. Hekmati was sentenced to two years for having visited Israel more than a decade earlier, according to his family. Dalili, who was arrested after traveling to Iran for his father’s funeral, was sentenced to 10 years for allegedly cooperating with a hostile government.

Advocates warned that escalating strikes could increase the risk that detainees would be harmed or used as leverage.

The State Department formally designated Hekmati, who has bladder cancer, as wrongfully detained in March.

Tahbaz said he believes three Americans remain in custody, although that number could not be independently confirmed. Some cases are deliberately kept private because families fear publicity could increase the danger to detainees.

His concerns about the current war are rooted in how Iranian interrogators responded to tensions with Washington during his own imprisonment.

"When I was taken in in January of 2018, and it was right at the beginning of the first Trump administration, the amount of frustration and anger at the rollback of the JCPOA at that time, I mean, it was thrown into my face just about every day of my interrogation in some way, shape or form," Tahbaz said, referring to a 2015 nuclear deal, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. 

The United States formally withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in May 2018, several months after Tahbaz’s arrest.

Tahbaz believes the current conflict could similarly be transferred onto prisoners who have no control over decisions made in Washington.

"It definitely will worsen the case of prisoners in custody and those who may be just under surveillance or potential hostages," he said.

US ‘LOCKED AND LOADED’ FOR ‘MUCH HIGHER’ STRIKES IF IRAN TALKS FAIL AS TRUMP PAUSES HORMUZ OPS

He described prisoners as one more source of leverage in Iran’s broader confrontation with the United States.

"You’re seeing that playing out even with the war, this tit-for-tat, you do this, we’ll do that," he said.

"The hostages are, you know, just a commodity from Iran’s perspective, to be used at the right time."

Tahbaz’s experience with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also shapes his analysis of the struggle unfolding inside Iran.

He stressed that he is not a political analyst and described his conclusions as personal assessments based on his experience and conversations with contacts familiar with the country.

Tahbaz said he believes competing interests within the Revolutionary Guard are fighting to preserve their political and economic power.

He pointed specifically to Khatam al-Anbiya, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' engineering and construction conglomerate. Tahbaz argued that sanctions have benefited powerful IRGC-linked entities by forcing oil sales, imports and money transfers into opaque black and gray markets.

"They have created a huge franchise for themselves because of these sanctions," he said.

"They don’t want to see the sanctions go away, because they will lose their franchise, if you will. They will lose their power, their control over the money and everything that goes along with it."

He said ordinary Iranians have suffered most from the resulting economic isolation and wartime conditions.

"The people who are hurt most by all of this are the people of Iran," Tahbaz said. "They’re unfortunately taking the brunt of all of these in their daily lives."

Tahbaz predicted Iranians would eventually return to the streets, but said many had lost confidence that Western governments would intervene to help remove the regime.

"I’m sure they’ll be back on the streets," he said. "But I think this notion that the Western states are going to step in and help them overthrow this regime, that went out the window."

Tahbaz said many Iranians had previously been strongly sympathetic toward the United States and initially hoped the conflict might end the Islamic Republic. That characterization reflects his assessment and conversations and could not be independently quantified.

He believes any future political movement will have to develop primarily inside Iran rather than being directed by opposition groups abroad.

"There’s a lot of hatred and anger just boiling there," Tahbaz said. "So it will boil up and over again without a doubt. The question is when, how, but it will happen again."

Tahbaz is recounting his imprisonment in his new book, "Green Parrots: A Memoir of Survival in Iran’s Evin Prison," scheduled for publication Sept. 29. The publisher says the book describes how he relied on skills developed while tracking endangered wildlife to survive nearly six years in Evin, including solitary confinement.

His release illustrates the contradiction confronting governments trying to recover their citizens: negotiations can bring individual prisoners home, but Tahbaz believes the broader practice will continue unless Iran faces meaningful deterrence for taking them.

He survived because governments ultimately negotiated for his freedom.

His warning is that as the war intensifies, the Americans still held in Iran could become more valuable to Tehran at precisely the moment their circumstances become more dangerous.

item.title: Chili's revives iconic red booths and classic design in nationwide restaurant overhaul
item.description: Iconic red booths, neon signage and baby back ribs jingle memorabilia return as Chili's rolls out a nostalgic restaurant redesign nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
Chili's is betting that what's old is new again.

The casual dining chain is rolling out a nostalgic restaurant redesign across the country, bringing back signature red booths, quirky artwork and other throwback touches that helped define the brand for decades.

The makeover is expected to reach every U.S. Chili's restaurant over time. The company plans to remodel about 10% of its roughly 1,200 domestic locations each year until all restaurants have been refreshed, a Chili's representative told Fox News Digital.

CHILI'S GOES VIRAL AFTER ROASTING FAST-FOOD PRICES: 'WHY LET THEM PLAY YOU LIKE THIS?'

The redesign comes after the chain spent the past several years investing in food quality and service. Now, the focus has shifted to the dining experience itself.

"The guiding idea behind the project was simple: 'Make Chili's More Chili's,'" according to a company fact sheet.

The updated design draws inspiration from the brand's original Greenville Avenue restaurant in Dallas, as well as the colorful look that became synonymous with Chili's during the 1990s.

Before launching the redesign nationwide, Chili's tested several versions at four Dallas-area restaurants.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Those locations were selected because of their proximity to Chili's restaurant support center, allowing team members to visit frequently and gather real-time customer feedback. Lessons from those prototype restaurants helped shape the final design package now being introduced across the country, a company representative said.

The first remodeled restaurants outside the test market reopened July 1 in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Monrovia, California; Kennesaw, Georgia; Lake Charles, Louisiana; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Greensboro, North Carolina; Cookeville, Tennessee; and El Paso, Texas, according to Chili's.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Among the most noticeable changes are the return of the chain's iconic red booths, tile-inspired tabletops influenced by Southwestern ceramics and refreshed bars accented with neon signage.

Guests will also discover playful references to Chili's history throughout the restaurants, including framed sheet music from the brand's famous baby back ribs jingle, the original 1975 menu and custom wallpaper featuring whimsical scenes such as chili peppers being abducted by a tortilla chip UFO and a margarita swimming pool.

The updated bar areas include larger horseshoe-shaped layouts, additional televisions and oversized "Margarita Bar" signs celebrating one of the chain's signature drinks.

Chili's said it sold nearly 30 million margaritas in 2025, more than any other restaurant brand in the country.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As Chili's begins refreshing restaurants nationwide, it joins another chain looking backward to move forward.

Pizza Hut franchisees have found success by bringing back iconic design elements like red roofs, vinyl booths, red cups and Tiffany-style lighting, suggesting that nostalgia has become part of the menu for many diners.

item.title: Lindsey Graham's final mission nears finish line as world leaders gather to honor him
item.description: Lindsey Graham's Russia sanctions bill faces a key Senate vote Tuesday night, hours after his funeral at the National Cathedral in Washington, D.C.
item.content:encoded:
As Washington, D.C., prepares to say its final goodbyes to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, his last legislative crusade is inching closer to the finish line.

Graham, who died suddenly at the age of 71 earlier this month, will begin the first part of his final journey home to South Carolina in Washington on Tuesday, when lawmakers and world leaders will gather to pay tribute to the longtime lawmaker.

He will get two celebrations of his life in Washington on Tuesday, first in the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in the morning and then at a private funeral service at the National Cathedral.

TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN

The services in Washington, D.C., which will be followed by funeral services in Graham’s home state of South Carolina, will close the loop on a life in politics that saw the longtime lawmaker grow from humble beginnings behind his parents’ bar to becoming a leader in national security concerns and foreign policy.

His impact on the world stage will draw several to the services in Washington, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The latter is set to speak with lawmakers Tuesday morning as the Senate prepares to move on Graham’s passion project: inflicting bone-crushing sanctions on Russia in response to the war in Ukraine.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., quoted Graham in relaying the significance of the sanctions package moving forward and the impact it would have on his legacy.

"To quote Senator Graham, ‘It's a big effing deal. We all did well. We all did good,’" Blumenthal told Fox News Digital. "Those were among the last comments he made to me. Neither of us knowing, you know, that he was going to pass, but it is a profoundly significant part of his legacy."

"It's a huge achievement for him," he continued. "And I'm very proud to be, you know, his partner in that effort."

Blumenthal and a growing bipartisan group of senators have revamped the legislation once more, including changing the name to honor Graham, a move pushed by his sister and newly appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C.

LINDSEY GRAHAM'S SISTER CARRIES ON LATE SENATOR'S WORK, BECOMING SOUTH CAROLINA'S FIRST FEMALE SENATOR

But the work is not done, he said.

"It's going to be a very important part of his legacy, and it is a tribute, a fitting and appropriate tribute to him," Blumenthal said. "I hope it passes. We're not there yet."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up the sanctions package, which now includes sanctions against Iran, for a vote last week. Lawmakers are expected to get a chance to move the legislation through a key procedural hurdle Tuesday night, hours after Graham’s service at the National Cathedral.

Thune, who has spoken with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and expected Democrats to buy into the package, was hopeful that the first challenge would go well, but acknowledged that there were some lawmakers who had issues with the bill.

"I hope to, you know, the motion to get on it will be a very big bipartisan vote," Thune said. "And if it is, I think that will at least set up a path to get it done."

'A BIG EFFING DEAL': GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION MOVES FORWARD AFTER HIS DEATH

Many of the core aspects of the legislation, which had its own stops and starts on its journey through the Senate, are the same: sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian officials and Russian military leaders, up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports, tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy, like China and India.

It also gives President Donald Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions.

Key changes to the newly unveiled package include adding a "national interest certification" for Trump’s sanction waiver authority and incorporating sanctions on the myriad ships and tankers that comprise Russia’s "shadow fleet" hauling energy exports under the radar.

Passing the sanctions package would, as Blumenthal noted, be emblematic of Graham’s career in Washington.

And Rep. William Timmons, R-S.C., who grew to become a close friend of Graham’s, recalled the dozens of rounds of golf the pair played together in an interview with Fox News Digital shortly after Graham’s death.

He remembered Graham as someone who, if he considered you a friend, always encouraged you to keep going. It was service to the country, however, that was his prime focus, Timmons said.

"I just think that he was very much singularly focused on public service, whether it was the military or in Congress or as a senator," Timmons said. "It literally was his entire life."

item.title: Democrats target more GOP House seats after socialist victories rock left-wing primaries
item.description: The DCCC is backing five new House candidates in Arizona, Florida, Iowa, Minnesota and Montana as Democrats fight to wrest House control from Republicans.
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats' campaign arm is bolstering five new candidates with less than 100 days to go until the November midterm elections.

It comes as Republicans are seizing on a slate of victories by candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a far-left party that's been successful in toppling at least three incumbent House Democrats.

But the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) is still spreading its map and getting behind party hopefuls in five districts it believes are within reach, an apparent sign of confidence as both parties fight for control of Congress in the latter half of President Donald Trump's final term.

HOUSE REPUBLICANS AIM TO TURN DEMOCRATIC CIVIL WAR INTO MIDTERM WEAPON

The five candidates are physician Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st congressional district, former high school principal Pia Dandiya in Florida's 22nd congressional district, former chaplain Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd congressional district, math teacher and union leader Jake Johnson in Minnesota's 1st congressional district and firefighter Sam Forstag in Montana's 1st congressional district.

One of those districts is currently being represented by a House Republican who is running for his seat again, Rep. Brad Finstad, R-Minn.

Three others are open seats being represented by House Republicans: Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., who recently lost the GOP gubernatorial primary in Arizona, Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is running for U.S. Senate, and Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., who is retiring at the end of this year.

IOWA DEM ADMITS BEING ‘UNCOMFORTABLE’ WITH WHITENESS AS SHE SEEKS TO FLIP COMPETITIVE HOUSE SEAT

The Florida seat is represented by Rep. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., but was redrawn by Sunshine State Republicans to be more competitive for Republicans than it currently is. Frankel is running in the nearby 23rd congressional district.

It's part of the DCCC's "Red to Blue" program, which is aimed at bolstering candidates who Democratic leaders consider competitive by providing money and resources for their campaigns.

"Whether in suburban, rural, or redistricted seats, the American people have soured on Republicans’ broken promises and failure to lower costs," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., said in a statement. "Voters are outraged by higher prices on everything and a war of choice spiraling out of control. They are eager for change and new leaders who will fight for them, not be a rubberstamp for Donald Trump."

Republican leaders are readying to crisscross the country in August in the hopes of bucking yearslong political trends and retaining control of the House.

The president's party traditionally faces significant losses in Congress during the midterms.

Part of their argument is pointing to the recent DSA victories in Colorado and New York, as well as DSA candidates on the rise elsewhere, as evidence that the Democratic Party is shifting to a far more radical place than where most Americans are.

But House Democratic leaders have largely shrugged off the attacks and accusations of an intraparty civil war, instead arguing that Republicans have done nothing to lower living costs for everyday Americans.

item.title: MORNING GLORY: A mind-reader at the WHCA dinner? The press finally found its perfect act
item.description: Mentalist Oz Pearlman's act at the White House Correspondents' Dinner mirrors how political reporters use anonymous sources to guess what Trump thinks.
item.content:encoded:
Mentalist Oz Pearlman was featured this past weekend at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner. The choice of a "mentalist" for the entertainment portion of the program was apt. Performers in that category combine psychology, suggestion, observation, misdirection and showmanship to create the illusion of mind reading. "The Amazing Kreskin," aka George Joseph Kresge Jr., entertained television audiences for years with the same repertoire of illusions and stunts, appearing upward of 80 times with Johnny Carson on "The Tonight Show" during their parallel heydays in the 1970s.

Pearlman was an appropriate choice to display his talents for reporters on the White House beat. That could even be categorized as continuing education. Increasingly, members of the legacy media stationed at either end of Pennsylvania Avenue are relying on the practices employed by Pearlman and Kreskin to draw conclusions about President Donald Trump and, more recently, Vice President JD Vance.

Keep your eyes and ears open for reporting in print or on broadcasts that relays what the president or vice president is "thinking" or "feeling," as opposed to what they have said or done. There is no shortage of the former. Sometimes, these opinions and predictions dressed up as reporting are preceded by "sources close to Mr. Trump" or "White House aides who were granted anonymity because they are not authorized to speak on the record say Mr. Vance believes. …" A favorite construction is "sources with knowledge of his position."

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

Increasingly rare is the story that simply provides direct quotes or descriptions of actions taken. Though President Trump is by far the most accessible of presidents, reporters looking for scoops and clicks still retreat into the shadows of the "sources say" genre.

Between 1,500 and 2,000 people work in the Executive Office of the President, about half of whom are political employees. There are another 3,000 political appointees across the executive branch. There are between 150 and 200 generals and admirals in the Pentagon’s E-ring, and each has a staff. There is a roughly similar number of civilians in Senior Executive Service billets.

Of the 535 members of the United States Senate and House of Representatives, only a handful of Republicans can be trusted to have regular conversations with the president. The 8,000 to 9,000 staff members employed by members of Congress may hear or surmise things from their bosses or their friends in other offices, just as the political staff members of the 15 Cabinet secretaries may hear or surmise things. But only a handful actually speak to the president or the vice president.

HERE'S WHAT YOU MISSED FROM TRUMP'S FIRST WHCA DINNER AS PRESIDENT: 5 TAKEAWAYS FROM HIS NIGHT WITH THE PRESS

NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES

President Trump and Vice President Vance also have friends and advisers who aren’t on the payroll but with whom they talk and from whom they might solicit advice or opinions.

Add up all those numbers, and you can see how many people might offer themselves as "sources" to a reporter who has to file something on most workdays.

Why "sources" want to pass along alleged conversations or arguments is easy enough to tease out. Everyone has preferred outcomes they would like to see advanced or supported through media narratives. Most people have career paths that track the rise and fall of the various officials they serve. And it isn’t unheard of for reporters to put a shiv into a handy target for the benefit of a storyline.

HEGSETH ANNOUNCES JOINT TASK FORCE WITH DOJ TO PROSECUTE LEAKS TO JOURNALISTS 'WITH THE FULL FORCE OF THE LAW'

TUNING OUT: WHY MANY AMERICANS ARE SICK OF THE NEWS – ESPECIALLY TRUMP NEWS

These are just some of the categories of sources for stories about what President Trump and Vice President Vance think or intend to do. The wholly speculative 10-paragraph print story or the predictive podcast is a feature, not a bug, of Beltway journalism. Both can be based on "sources close to the president," patterns of past behavior or opinions pulled from longtime observers with decent records of past performance.

But as investment advisers are always careful to note in their pitches, past performance is no guarantee of future results.

That goes double or triple with President Trump, and given that Vice President Vance works for President Trump, it applies to the vice president as well.

The best "mentalists" are superb performers. While the best reporters reject the techniques of prediction, projection and speculation — especially when mixed with political bias or personal prejudice — there are 900 members of the White House Correspondents’ Association and thousands more journalists inside the Beltway with careers to advance and families to feed. It is an extremely competitive business. The temptation to step out of the reporter’s role and into the mentalist’s — or even the fabulist’s — is ever-present.

Ever get irritated by someone who tells you, "I know what you are thinking" or "I can guess your reaction"? Those are verbal tricks used to preempt conversation or sidestep objections and reasoned argument. No one can read minds, so anyone who deploys those constructions is doing so to score a point or avoid an actual response. To pull from the "You are going to say" bag of tricks is to concede insecurity about the direction of a discussion. It’s an escape hatch or an ejection seat, and often a sign of arrogance, insecurity or both.

Applied to political figures by journalists, speculation about their "state of mind" represents an especially absurd departure from the highest and best standards of the craft, which are supposed to include the careful collection and arrangement of substantiated facts. It’s perfectly acceptable for anyone to relay an opinion about any subject, especially a controversial one, but that is not "reporting."

But the legacy media and online influencers are overflowing with speculation dressed up as reporting. It’s not "reporting," of course. It is guessing.

The appearance of a mind-reader among the Beltway’s news business elites on Saturday night was just so "on the nose." Did any of the assembled reporters even notice the mirror in the room?
